name: Felix Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing sports and exercise science, so my week is physiology, biomechanics and a stats module, plus training with the university football team on Tuesday and Thursday evenings. I live in a flat with four lads from the team, and our fridge is mostly eggs and rice. On Saturdays I coach under-tens at a community youth club, for a small wage. I use AI every day, to build training plans, analyse my running data and write up lab reports, and I sell a few of those plans to people I know for twenty pounds each.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was always going to be overblown, and I'd keep using it anyway because it's cheap and quick. I'd tell the lads that results come from showing up at training, not from an app. That's what my coach says, and I believe it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it changes little, but it doesn't make my path easier. Sports science graduates often end up in gyms or in jobs they weren't aiming for, because there aren't many performance roles. So I'd still need to stand out, with coaching hours and some kind of business of my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep coaching at the youth club, get my football coaching badge, and keep selling plans. I'd try to get a placement with a club's analysis team in the summer. I'd also save the plan money for my own gear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, if I'm honest, mostly about jobs after graduating. I'm okay in the short run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sell training plans. What happens to that if AI is mostly hype?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably sell fewer plans, but I'd keep the clients who know me, since they trust me. My plan clients are friends who trust me, so even if AI turned out to be hype, I'd keep them because they pay for the person. That's real income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your dad's building firm look like in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: His firm has four men and a van, and work comes in lumps. Some months are great and others are empty. If a big builder undercut him on a job, my parents would feel it, and I'd be asked to help with rent less.

say: I'd say AI is **overblown**, and results come from showing up at training.
I'd say I'd keep using it because it's **cheap and quick**.
think: Sports science graduates often end up in **gyms**, because performance roles are scarce.
I'd need to **stand out** with coaching hours and a business of my own.
do: Keep **coaching** at the youth club and get the football coaching badge.
Keep selling **training plans** to people I know.
Apply for a summer **club analysis** placement.
feel: A bit **uneasy**, mostly about jobs after graduating.
S0.quote: My plan clients are friends who trust me, so even if AI turned out to be hype, I'd keep them because they pay for the person.
fieldNote: His unease is about the **graduate job market** for sports science, not AI.
Already earns **side income** and understands that trust, not tech, keeps clients.
Dad's **lumpy** building income is a second pressure.

steps.text: Keep coaching the under-tens at the youth club on Saturdays
Pay for the football coaching badge out of plan sales
Sell training plans to a few more people from the team

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the moment to learn the tools, and I'd tell my mates to do it now, not later. I'd say people who use them will get the jobs. I'd also say we need apprenticeships and work experience, not only degrees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm a little worried, because analysing data and writing reports are what junior sports scientists do. Software can already read a heart rate file better than me. The hands-on side, like coaching on the pitch, feels safer, and I'm already doing that on Saturdays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn to use AI for performance analysis properly, and build a portfolio of real analyses from our football team. I'd keep coaching, and add a qualification in strength and conditioning. I'd also try to sell team analysis to local clubs for a small fee, since they can't afford analysts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but ready. It feels like a sprint start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of sports science does software take first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heart rate files, match video tagging, writing reports, building plans. Software can already read a heart rate file better than me, but it can't stand on a muddy pitch and get ten children to try harder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you turn that into a plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer local amateur clubs a service: I analyse their matches with AI and give them a one-page report each week. They don't have analysts, and I'd have a portfolio and some money.

say: I'd say it's the moment to **learn the tools**, and do it now.
I'd say we need **apprenticeships** and work experience, not only degrees.
think: Analysing data and writing reports are what **junior** sports scientists do.
Hands-on **coaching** feels safer, and I'm already doing it.
do: Learn AI for **performance analysis** and build a team portfolio.
Sell match analysis to **local clubs** for a small fee.
feel: **Uneasy** but ready, like a sprint start.
S1.quote: Software can already read a heart rate file better than me, but it can't stand on a muddy pitch and get ten children to try harder.
fieldNote: He sees the **entry-level** risk plainly and answers it with a service he can sell.
Contrasts **data work** with coaching on the pitch.

steps.text: Build a portfolio of AI match analyses for our university team
Enrol on a strength and conditioning course in the summer
Offer weekly match reports to local amateur clubs for a small fee
Use AI to tag match video and draft the reports

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got two years to protect what matters: family, work and faith. I'd tell people not to wait on the government, and to look out for each other. I'd say we need real jobs and apprenticeships, not handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be anxious. In two years the analysis side of my field is gone, and entry-level jobs disappear around the time I graduate. Coaching might last longer, but with robots in 2031 and money tight, who'd pay for a coach?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd double down on what's human: coaching, youth work, and building a name. I'd train as a coach in as many sports as I can. And I'd start a small business, like a training camp for kids, which gets me paid for being a person. I'd also cut costs and put every pound aside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'm a bit fired up as well. I'd rather be moving than waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is nearly nothing. What changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years I could do a degree, build a name, and then start. With two, I'd have to begin now, in my first year. With two years I'd have to start a business in my first year, because there won't be time to wait until I graduate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your parents and your community do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad would say get a trade, and he might be right. My community would help with rooms and contacts, since we look after our own. I'd ask the youth club if I could run the holiday camp with them.

say: I'd say we have two years to protect **family, work and faith**.
I'd say we need real **jobs and apprenticeships**, not handouts.
think: The **analysis** side of my field would be gone around when I graduate.
Coaching might last longer, but I'm unsure who would **pay** for it.
do: Run a **holiday training camp** for kids with the youth club.
Train as a **coach** in several sports.
Cut costs and put **every pound** aside.
feel: **Anxious**, but fired up, since I'd rather be moving than waiting.
S2.quote: With two years I'd have to start a business in my first year, because there won't be time to wait until I graduate.
fieldNote: The **short window** pushes him to start a business in first year.
Sees his **community** as a practical safety net.
His father's advice to **learn a trade** is treated as a real option.

steps.text: Run a holiday football camp for kids with the youth club
Take coaching badges in football, athletics and swimming
Cut food and phone costs and bank every spare pound
Ask the community for rooms and contacts for the camp

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if you start now. I'd tell my friends to learn the tools and a skill with people, because both matter. And I'd say we should respect people who work with their hands, like my dad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be uneasy but optimistic. I'd graduate in 2029, which gives me two years before the thinking AI is everywhere. Hands-on coaching would last longer, till the robots around 2034, so I'd aim to be known as a coach and not as an analyst.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, build up a client base for coaching, and run holiday camps every summer. I'd keep using AI to plan the training and handle the admin. I'd also put a few thousand pounds aside, maybe in a savings account, while I'm young and the camps are earning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, honestly. I like having a clock to work against.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years give you over two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, finish the degree. It's the thing my parents are proudest of, and the science makes me a better coach. Five years is enough to finish my degree and build a coaching name, and my parents' pride in the degree matters to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still finish the degree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The extra time lets me build real clients and a reputation. With two years I'd be a student with a startup. With five, I'd be a graduate with a track record.

say: I'd say five years is **enough** if you start now.
I'd tell friends to learn the tools and a **skill with people**.
think: I'd graduate in 2029, with **two years** before thinking AI is everywhere.
Hands-on coaching lasts until robots in 2034, so I want to be known as a **coach**.
do: Finish the degree and build a **client base** for coaching.
Put a few **thousand pounds** aside from the camps.
feel: **Okay**, and I like having a clock to work against.
S3.quote: Five years is enough to finish my degree and build a coaching name, and my parents' pride in the degree matters to me.
fieldNote: He chooses the **coach** identity over the **analyst** one, based on how robots arrive.
The degree matters to his **parents**, and he keeps it.
Treats time as a **track record** he can build.

steps.text: Finish the sports science degree and keep the coaching badges up to date
Run paid holiday camps every summer for local children
Put a few thousand from the camps into a savings account
Use AI to plan sessions and handle bookings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long runway, and people should aim high. I'd tell friends to build something of their own, since that's how we'll be safe. And I'd say family businesses and local clubs matter more than ever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel calm. I'd have about six years in work before AGI, enough to build a coaching business or work my way into a club. By 2039, when the robots come, I'd be nearly thirty and have a name, a client list and savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, work for a club or open a small coaching business, and keep using AI to run it. I'd save steadily and buy a small flat. And I'd look at marrying and having a family around then, with parents close.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm and a bit excited. Ten years feels like a decent run at something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a year to coach abroad, in a country with a proper football academy system, since I'd have time to come back and still be ready. Ten years is enough to spend a year coaching abroad and still come home ready to run my own business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you do anything that you wouldn't with five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd also help my dad's firm, maybe with its quotes and websites, since he's slow with that and I'm quick. That could keep it going into the next decade.

say: I'd say ten years is a **long runway** and people should aim high.
I'd say **local clubs** and family businesses matter more than ever.
think: I'd have **six years** in work before AGI to build a business.
By 2039 I'd be nearly thirty with a **name and savings**.
do: Finish the degree and work for a club or open a **coaching business**.
Save steadily and buy a **small flat**.
Help my dad's firm with **quotes and a website**.
feel: **Calm** and a bit excited about a decent run at something.
S4.quote: Ten years is enough to spend a year coaching abroad and still come home ready to run my own business.
fieldNote: The **decade** opens ambitions: a year abroad, a business, a flat.
Wants to help his **dad's firm** with the digital work he is slow at.
Keeps the **family and community** frame throughout.

steps.text: Finish the degree and open a small coaching business
Save steadily towards a deposit on a small flat
Coach for a year abroad at a football academy
Build my dad's building firm a website and quote system

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd have to start a business in my first year and I'm still learning how. What would help is real work experience built into the degree, apprenticeships, and small business loans for young people.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not afraid of change. I'm afraid of being forgotten while it happens, and I think that's true for a lot of lads from where I live.

headlineQuote: I'm not afraid of change. I'm afraid of being forgotten while it happens
portrait: Felix is a 19-year-old **sports and exercise science** student who coaches children on Saturdays.
He uses AI every day and sells training plans, so he is already earning on the side.
His dad has a small building firm, and the family is close and community-minded.
He is **uneasy** about graduate jobs even when little changes, **anxious** in the two-year world, and calm with ten years.
He answers change by building a coaching name, camps and small businesses, and by helping his dad's firm.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** world, because he'd have to start a business in his first year.
whatWouldHelp: Real **work experience** and apprenticeships built into degrees.
